papers.title_in_file: Simulating Work Extraction in a Dinuclear Quantum Battery Using a Variational Quantum Algorithm
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Section I introduction, Section III results discussion (noise and temperature paragraphs), Section IV conclusion, Appendix A noise model; the Hamiltonian and ergotropy derivations in Section II were skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: A Qiskit simulation study of a variational quantum algorithm for optimal work extraction in a dinuclear copper(II) quantum battery model, with and without a noise model.

assertions.value: The authors report that variational quantum algorithms can reproduce key trends in experimental data for the dinuclear quantum battery model.
quotes: Our results demonstrate that variational quantum algorithms can reproduce key trends in experimental data
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result from one study; the comparison is to one published experimental data set.
assertions.reader_inference: The conclusion words this as reasonable agreement, a weaker claim than the abstract.

assertions.value: The authors simulate the optimal work extraction protocol for a dinuclear quantum battery, in both noiseless and noisy conditions, using variational quantum algorithms simulated with IBM Qiskit.
quotes: We simulate the optimal work extraction protocol proposed in [9], for a two-cell (dinuclear) quantum battery, in both noiseless and noisy conditions
Variational Quantum Algorithms simulated using IBM Qiskit [55]
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its method, Section I, p.2.
assertions.reader_inference: The noise is a simulated noise model (Appendix A), not a run on physical quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that the presence of a noisy environment hinders the accuracy of the evaluation of the amount of energy stored in the system.
quotes: We have shown that the presence of a noisy environment hinders the accuracy of the evaluation of the amount of energy stored in the system.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result under one noise model.

assertions.value: The authors report that the protocol is highly precise only at low temperatures and that its accuracy at ambient conditions remains limited; in the noiseless simulation they report performance degradation observed close to 100 K.
quotes: the protocol is highly precise only at low temperatures, and its accuracy at ambient conditions remains limited, compromising its usability
the simulation of the work extraction protocol exhibits high precision only at lower temperatures, with performance degradation observed close to 100 K
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result from one study.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum-assisted Gaussian process regression using random Fourier features
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Section I introduction, start of Section II, the numerical-simulation part of Section IV, Section V conclusion; the circuit construction in Section III was not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: A quantum-assisted algorithm for sparse Gaussian process regression based on random Fourier feature kernel approximation, with a complexity argument and a classical-simulator demonstration.

assertions.value: The authors state that they achieve a polynomial-order computational speedup relative to the classical method.
quotes: We achieve a polynomialorder computational speedup relative to the classical method.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement from a complexity argument; not a run on hardware.
assertions.reader_inference: The speedup is a computational-complexity comparison; the size of the quantum data-loading and read-out cost under the algorithm's assumptions was not assessed by this reader.

assertions.value: The authors report a simulation experiment with N = 16 data measurements, used to approximate the function f (x) = sin(x).
quotes: Our experiment used N = 16 data measurements with
to approximate the function f (x) = sin(x).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its simulation setup, Section IV.
assertions.reader_inference: The demonstration is a small circuit simulation on a classical computer, not a hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors state that the variance of the approximations is distant from the expected variance, and that the constraints of simulating qubits on a classical computer require the use of a small approximation parameter.
quotes: However, the variance of the approximations is distant from the expected variance.
the constraints of simulating qubits on a classical computer require the use of a small approximation parameter.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of a limit of its simulation, Section IV.

assertions.value: The authors state that their algorithm is susceptible to the time parameter t in simulations and that a careful selection of t is important to run the model successfully.
quotes: Our algorithm is susceptible to the time parameter t in simulations. A careful selection of t is important to run the model successfully.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of a limit, Section V.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Natural Language Processing based Sentiment Analysis using lambeq Toolkit
papers.what_it_is: A short study of binary sentiment classification with the lambeq QNLP toolkit, in classical, noiseless quantum, JAX and noisy simulated-quantum pipelines.

assertions.value: The authors report that perfect accuracy on the test set was achieved for three simulations and that a decent accuracy was obtained for the noisy quantum pipeline case.
quotes: Perfect accuracy on the test set was achieved for three simulations and a decent accuracy was obtained for the noisy quantum pipeline case.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one small data set.
assertions.reader_inference: The test set holds 30 sentences, so perfect accuracy rests on a very small sample. One of the three perfect-accuracy runs is the classical pipeline, so the claim covers two quantum simulations, not three.

assertions.value: The authors report a data set of 130 sentences, with 70 in the training set, 30 in the development set and 30 in the test set.
quotes: The dataset consists of 130 sentences, out of which 70 are in the training set, 30 in development set and 30 in test set.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its data set, Section III.C.

assertions.value: The authors report 83.33% accuracy on the test set for the noisy quantum pipeline, run on Qiskit's fake quantum hardware backend called FakeVigo.
quotes: We achieved 83.33% accuracy on the test set.
we have used Qiskit's fake quantum hardware backend called FakeVigo
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract says experiments ran on a noisy quantum device, but the body says a fake-backend simulator was used; no physical device run is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that QNLP is a new field and that much work needs to be done in this field in order to achieve quantum advantage.
quotes: QNLP is a new field and much work needs to be done in this field in order to achieve quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of a limit, Section V.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no quantum-versus-classical advantage; the classical pipeline also reached perfect test accuracy.

papers.title_in_file: Adversarial Quantum Machine Learning: An Information-Theoretic Generalization Analysis
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction and contributions, problem setup, Assumption 1 and Theorems 2 to 5 and their discussion, the numerical-experiments section; the proofs in the appendices were not read.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that derives information-theoretic upper bounds on the generalization error of quantum classifiers trained against bounded-norm white-box adversarial attacks, checked on a synthetic example.

assertions.value: The authors derive novel information-theoretic upper bounds on the generalization error of adversarially trained quantum classifiers, and state that the second term of the bound scales linearly with the adversarial perturbation size.
quotes: we derive novel information-theoretic upper bounds on the generalization error of adversarially trained quantum classifiers
the second term scales linearly with
perturbation size ε.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as proved theorems under Assumption 1, Theorems 2 and 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the bounds hold under Assumption 1, which requires the quantum embeddings to be sufficiently noisy, and on stated upper bounds for the perturbation; they leave tighter bounds outside that regime as an open problem.
quotes: These results hold under Assumption 1, which requires the quantum embeddings to be sufficiently noisy, and on the stated upper bounds for the perturbation
We leave it as an open problem to establish tighter bounds in this regime.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the scope of its results, after Theorem 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in the presence of a training-test mismatch of the adversary, training with a strong adversary is the preferred strategy, as weak training adversaries may incur a positive non-vanishing term.
quotes: We show that in the presence of this training-test mismatch, training with a strong adversary is the preferred strategy, as weak training adversaries may incur a positive non-vanishing term
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the upper bound of Theorem 5; a bound, not a lower bound.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement rests on upper bounds, so it shows what the bound guarantees, not that a weak training adversary always fails.

assertions.value: The authors report numerical experiments in a synthetic setting; where their stated assumption is not satisfied, they state that their bound (20) is loose and leave tighter bounds as an open problem.
quotes: Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with numerical experiments for a synthetic setting.
our bound (20) is loose. We leave it as an open problem
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result for one synthetic example.

papers.title_in_file: Investigating the Relation Between Problem Hardness and QUBO Properties
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, the experiments (Section 4) and conclusion; the Qubo derivations in Sections 2 and 3 were not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: An empirical study of how the spectral gap of Qubo formulations of clustering and SVM training correlates with properties of the original problem, such as data separability.

assertions.value: The authors report that the spectral gap of Clustering Qubo instances positively correlates with data separability, while for SVM Qubo the opposite is true.
quotes: An empirical evaluation provides interesting insights, showing that the spectral gap of Clustering Qubo instances positively correlates with data separability, while for SVM Qubo the opposite is true.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on synthetic data sets.

assertions.value: The authors report experiments on randomly sampled synthetic Cones and Circles data sets, with 1000 data sets sampled per setting and three problem sizes compared.
quotes: we sample 1000 different Cones data sets with varying cluster distances
A similar setup can be found in Fig. 5, where 1000 different Circles data sets are sampled
For every experiment, we compare three different problem sizes
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its experimental setup, Section 4.
assertions.reader_inference: The experiments are small synthetic instances; no quantum annealer run is reported in the parts read.

assertions.value: The authors state that, since different kernels are used, the exact correlation form depends on the exact data set and the used kernel.
quotes: Since different kernels are used in Fig. 4 and Fig. 5, the exact correlation form is dependent on the exact data set and the used kernel.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of a limit on its findings, Section 4.1.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the hardness of the original problems is not directly connected to solvability on quantum computers, and that it depends on the data set at hand and on specifics in the used Qubo formulation.
quotes: we conclude that the original problems' hardness is not directly connected to the solvability on quantum computers, as one might assume
it depends not only on the data set at hand, but also on specifics in the used Qubo formulation
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion drawn from two problem types and synthetic data.
assertions.reader_inference: The conclusion rests on spectral gap as the proxy for solvability and on two problems; it is not tested on a quantum annealer in the parts read.

quotes: the quantum principle is incorporated into deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to address the hardware limitations of conventional computers

papers.title_in_file: The Quantum Imitation Game: Reverse Engineering of Quantum Machine Learning Models
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, threat model, the worked examples and results discussion, conclusion; the reverse-engineering algorithm details were skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: A security paper that studies reverse engineering of transpiled quantum machine learning circuits by an untrusted cloud provider, and proposes dummy-gate countermeasures.

assertions.value: The authors assume the untrusted third-party quantum cloud provider is an adversary having white-box access to the transpiled version of the user-designed trained QML model during inference.
quotes: We assume the untrusted third-party quantum cloud provider is an adversary having white-box access to the transpiled version of the user-designed trained QML model during inference.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its threat model, Abstract.

assertions.value: The authors report that multi-qubit classifiers can be reverse-engineered under specific conditions with a mean error of order 10−2 in a reasonable time.
quotes: mean error of order 10−2 in a reasonable time
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from small classifiers in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The classifiers are small (one and two qubits in the worked examples), and the paper says the time grows considerably with qubit count.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in one worked example, the original model has a training accuracy of 69.47% and the reverse-engineered QML model has an accuracy of 67.22%.
quotes: has a training accuracy of ∼69.47%
has an accuracy of ∼67.22%
assertions.certainty_reason: A single worked example.
assertions.reader_inference: The reverse-engineered circuit in this case is not exactly the original design, so the attack recovered a functionally close model, not the exact parameters.

assertions.value: The authors propose adding dummy rotation gates with fixed parameters to increase the reverse-engineering overhead, and report that adding 2 dummy qubits and 2 layers increases the overhead, for a classifier with 2 qubits and 3 layers with a performance overhead of less than 9%.
quotes: We also propose adding dummy rotation gates in the QML model with fixed parameters to increase the RE overhead for defense.
For instance, an addition of 2 dummy qubits and 2 layers increases the overhead by
times for a classifier with 2 qubits and 3 layers with a performance overhead of less than 9%

assertions.reader_inference: The overhead multiple is in the abstract but its numeric glyph was not copied here.

papers.title_in_file: Do Quantum Circuit Born Machines Generalize?
papers.version_note: File is the arXiv v4 (May 2023) of the 2022 arXiv id; the record year is 2023.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, the key-concept review headings, the results discussion in Section III (selected paragraphs) and Section IV outlook; tables and appendices were not read.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of the generalization performance of quantum circuit Born machines (QCBMs) using a generalization evaluation framework, on a cardinality-constrained distribution.

assertions.value: The authors report that they investigate the QCBM's learning process of a cardinality-constrained distribution and see an increase in generalization performance while increasing the circuit depth.
quotes: We first investigate the QCBM's learning process of a cardinality-constrained distribution and see an increase in generalization performance while increasing the circuit depth.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one distribution family.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in the 12-qubit example, with as few as 30% of the valid data in the training set, the QCBM exhibits the best generalization performance toward generating unseen and valid data.
quotes: In the 12-qubit example presented here, we observe that with as few as 30% of the valid data in the training set, the QCBM exhibits the best generalization performance toward generating unseen and valid data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one 12-qubit example.
assertions.reader_inference: The 30% figure is the best of the training-set fractions tried in a single 12-qubit instance, not a general rule.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QCBM is able to effectively learn the reweighted dataset and generate unseen samples with higher quality than those in the training set.
quotes: We see that the QCBM is able to effectively learn the reweighted dataset and generate unseen samples with higher quality than those in the training set.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the 12-qubit circuit ansatz is executed on a quantum simulator, and that investigating the generalization performance of QCBMs on quantum hardware, and how noise impacts the training resources required, is future work.
quotes: the 12-qubit circuit ansatz with a line topology of parameterized gates for an even number of layers L is executed on a quantum simulator
it will be important to investigate the generalization performance of QCBMs on quantum hardware, and investigate how noise impacts the training resources required
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its setup and its limit, Fig. 1 and Section IV.
